bibl.title: Repetition Priming and Repetition Suppression: A Case for Enhanced Efficiency Through Neural Synchronization

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: In this Discussion Paper, we review four different theoretical proposals that have the potential to link repetition suppression and priming, with a particular focus on a proposal that stimulus repetition affects improved efficiency through enhanced neural synchronization.

span.label: repetition priming and repetition suppression
span.quote: Stimulus repetition in identification tasks leads to improved behavioral performance (“repetition priming”) but attenuated neural responses (“repetition suppression”) throughout task-engaged cortical regions.

span.label: review
span.quote: Below, we review four of the main theoretical proposals about what form these solutions might take (see also Grill-Spector et al., 2006).

span.label: The favoured synchrony account rests on very little direct empirical evaluation.
span.quote: Despite the promise that the synchrony model holds for resolving the puzzle of repetition priming and repetition suppression, there are relatively few studies that have evaluated it empirically.

span.label: Neither of the two surviving models has been subjected to a decisive set of tests, and the competing Bayesian account also has support.
span.quote: However, the Bayesian “explaining away” model has received experimental support, as well, and neither the synchrony nor “explaining away” model has been run through a full gauntlet of experimental tests.

span.label: The proposed MEG/ECoG evidence cannot be tied to repetition suppression, because field-activity measures have no established relation to overall activity level.
span.quote: One large downside in using source-estimated MEG or ECoG to assess changes in neural synchronization is that the analog of repetition suppression in these methods is unclear.

span.label: In the reply the authors concede that the Discussion Paper failed to make clear that the four models are not mutually exclusive.
span.quote: This is a point that we failed to clarify and that we fully endorse.

span.label: a CONTROL CONDITION against which spike-LFP coherence in the gamma range (30-80 Hz) was measured after adaptation
span.note: eliminates: that the change in synchronisation is a general property of the recording rather than an effect of stimulus repetition
span.quote: Spikes elicited by the test grating were simultaneously more synchronized with the local field potential (LFP) (spike-LFP coherence) in the gamma frequency range (30–80 Hz) relative to a control condition in which the adapting grating was replaced with a random dot patch of matched luminance.

span.label: the extreme form of the Explaining Away account was tested against the observed pattern of repetition suppression
span.note: eliminates: that ALL repetition suppression is high-level repetition expectation - the extreme version makes a prediction the data do not bear out
span.quote: This would appear to rule out the extreme version of the “explaining away” view in which all repetition-suppression effects are explained by relatively high-level repetition expectation.

span.label: repetition suppression
span.quote: However, the relationship between repetition priming and repetition suppression also presents a major puzzle: How is it that reductions in neural activity can mediate better behavioral performance

span.label: neural synchronization
span.quote: In this Discussion Paper, we review four different theoretical proposals that have the potential to link repetition suppression and priming, with a particular focus on a proposal that stimulus repetition affects improved efficiency through enhanced neural synchronization.

span.quote: In this Discussion Paper, we review four different theoretical proposals that have the potential to link repetition suppression and priming, with a particular focus on a proposal that stimulus repetition affects improved efficiency through enhanced neural synchronization.

span.label: sharpening
span.quote: A second idea, often referred to as “sharpening” (Desimone, 1996; Wiggs & Martin, 1998), holds that while neural activity is decreasing on the average, the decreases are carried mainly by the cells that are poorly tuned and/or weakly responsive to the repeated stimuli with the “best” cells (i.e., most selective/responsive) instead retaining their activity levels (Figure 1B).

span.label: Explaining Away
span.quote: Ewbank and Henson appear to take issue with our use of the label “Explaining Away” when referring to Friston’s Bayesian model, preferring instead “Predictive Coding”.

span.label: Predictive Coding
span.quote: Ewbank and Henson appear to take issue with our use of the label “Explaining Away” when referring to Friston’s Bayesian model, preferring instead “Predictive Coding”.

span.label: Explaining Away → Predictive Coding
span.note: A NAMING DISPUTE BETWEEN AUTHORS IN ONE EXCHANGE, AND NO TYPE HOLDS IT. `EWBANK AND HENSON APPEAR TO TAKE ISSUE WITH OUR USE OF THE LABEL “EXPLAINING AWAY” when referring to Friston's Bayesian model, PREFERRING INSTEAD “PREDICTIVE CODING”.` Two labels, one model, and the disagreement is printed rather than reconstructed. `renamed-across-fields` is the nearest type and it is wrong twice over: this is not across FIELDS and not a RENAME - both names are in current use by different authors in the same journal exchange, and neither replaced the other. `same-as` asserts an equivalence the disputants would both reject as missing the point, since the whole argument is about what the name must EXCLUDE (`a label that better distinguished the anti-symmetrical property ... from the variety of models that utilize prediction in very different ways`). **THE GATE REFUSED IT FOR A DIFFERENT REASON AND THE REFUSAL WAS STILL RIGHT**: `RENAMING` has `called / known as / termed / referred to as / the term / nomenclature` and not `label`. I measured `label` as a candidate cue before proposing it - **2 occurrences in renamed-across-fields edges against 65 in other edges, a 1.28% base rate**, against the ~0.00% the list's existing extensions were held to. Adding it would admit 65 edges that are not renamings. **Fifth missing relation type of the session**, after is-an-aspect-of, a-claim-about-a-usage, is-a-defining-condition-of and prerequisite-for. terminal-a, 2026-08-27.
span.quote: Ewbank and Henson appear to take issue with our use of the label “Explaining Away” when referring to Friston’s Bayesian model, preferring instead “Predictive Coding”.

span.label: **THE PUZZLE, STATED AS A PUZZLE, WHICH IS WHY THIS RECORD IS WORTH HAVING:** `How is it that REDUCTIONS IN NEURAL ACTIVITY CAN MEDIATE BETTER BEHAVIORAL PERFORMANCE?` **The corpus now holds four positions on that question, all merged today and none of them citing another in this set:** Desimone1996 calls suppression `an intrinsic property of visual cortical areas`; Carlesimo2004 reads an rCBF decrease as `the reduced neural activity needed to reprocess recently seen words`; mcmahon-olson2007 concludes suppression `ACCOMPANIES repetition priming but is UNLIKELY TO BE ITS CAUSE`; and this paper says the puzzle is real and rate is the wrong variable
span.quote: However, the relationship between repetition priming and repetition suppression also presents a major puzzle: How is it that reductions in neural activity can mediate better behavioral performance

span.label: **AND THE ANSWER IS A REPLY TO McMAHON AND OLSON RATHER THAN A CONTRADICTION OF THEM.** `as cells are firing at LOWER OVERALL RATES, they are firing MORE SYNCHRONOUSLY with one another, leading to more efficient neural processing` - and in simulation, `as the model's firing rates DECREASED with repetition, the synchronization of the spike times SIMULTANEOUSLY INCREASED.` **Both papers agree the rate drop is not the mechanism.** They differ on whether anything else in the same signal is: McMahon and Olson tested rate and selectivity and found neither sufficient; Gotts proposes a variable neither of them measured
span.quote: Importantly, as the model’s firing rates decreased with repetition, the synchronization of the spike times simultaneously increased.

span.label: **IT NAMES THE GAP IN ITS OWN EVIDENCE, WHICH A PROPOSAL PAPER USUALLY DOES NOT:** `despite exciting recent work on the role of neural synchronization in cognitive processes such as attention and perception, similar studies in the domain of learning and memory - and priming, in particular - have been LACKING.` **The mechanism is offered together with the statement that the direct evidence for it has not been collected in this domain.** Compare meyer1971's `At present we do not have ways to test all the possible explanations of these effects` - forty-one years apart, the same willingness to write the limitation flat
span.quote: We argue that despite exciting recent work on the role of neural synchronization in cognitive processes such as attention and perception, similar studies in the domain of learning and memory ––and priming, in particular––have been lacking.

span.label: `sharpening` - A NAMED ACCOUNT WHOSE NAME ENCODES ITS MECHANISM: `A second idea, OFTEN REFERRED TO AS “SHARPENING” (Desimone, 1996; Wiggs & Martin, 1998), holds that while neural activity is decreasing ON THE AVERAGE, the decreases are carried mainly by THE CELLS THAT ARE POORLY TUNED and/or weakly responsive ... with the “BEST” CELLS ... INSTEAD RETAINING THEIR ACTIVITY LEVELS.` THE WORD IS THE HYPOTHESIS: a population response gets NARROWER, not smaller, and the mean decrease that `repetition suppression` names is a side effect of that narrowing. Two names for one measurement, differing in what they say caused it.
span.quote: A second idea, often referred to as “sharpening” (Desimone, 1996; Wiggs & Martin, 1998), holds that while neural activity is decreasing on the average, the decreases are carried mainly by the cells that are poorly tuned and/or weakly responsive to the repeated stimuli with the “best” cells (i.e., most selective/responsive) instead retaining their activity levels (Figure 1B).

span.label: `priming` NARROWED BY STIPULATION - BUT NOT BY THIS PAPER'S AUTHORS: `the complex relationship between repetition suppression (RS) and BEHAVIORAL PRIMING (HENCEFORTH REFERRED TO AS PRIMING)`. **VOICE: this sentence is from a PEER COMMENTARY printed with the article, not from Gotts, Chow and Martin** - it opens `Gotts et al. present four neural models` and continues `I strongly support Gotts et al.'s call`. So the stipulation binds the COMMENTATOR's text, and a reader who takes it as the target article's own definition has attributed a narrowing to the wrong authors.
span.quote: Gotts et al. present four neural models designed to capture the complex relationship between repetition suppression (RS) and behavioral priming (henceforth referred to as priming).

span.label: `Explaining Away` / `Predictive Coding` - THE SAME MODEL, TWO LABELS, AND THE DISAGREEMENT IS PRINTED. `EWBANK AND HENSON APPEAR TO TAKE ISSUE WITH OUR USE OF THE LABEL “EXPLAINING AWAY” when referring to Friston's Bayesian model, PREFERRING INSTEAD “PREDICTIVE CODING”.` **This is a naming dispute conducted in the literature rather than reconstructed from it** - commentators object, authors answer, and both names go on being used. The authors' stated rationale is DISCRIMINATION: a label that separates the anti-symmetrical property from `the variety of models that utilize prediction in very different ways`. **Neither party thinks the model is in doubt; they disagree about what the name must exclude.**
span.quote: Ewbank and Henson appear to take issue with our use of the label “Explaining Away” when referring to Friston’s Bayesian model, preferring instead “Predictive Coding”.

span.label: `priming` / `repetition suppression` - TWO CORE TERMS WHOSE REFERENTS DIFFER BY ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE IN TIME. `The terms “PRIMING” and “REPETITION SUPPRESSION” are COMMONLY USED TO REFER TO PHENOMENA OCCURRING ON TIME SCALES THAT CAN DIFFER BY SEVERAL ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE, ranging from seconds to days or even years.` **The words are stable and what they denote is not.** A corpus joining two papers on `priming` may be joining a 200-millisecond effect to one lasting a year, and nothing in either paper's use of the word records which.
span.quote: The terms “priming” and “repetition suppression” are commonly used to refer to phenomena occurring on time scales that can differ by several orders of magnitude, ranging from seconds to days or even years.

span.label: builds-on → Gotts (2003) neocortical circuit model
span.quote: In a simplified neocortical circuit model that incorporated biologically proportionate numbers of excitatory and inhibitory cells and short-term plasticity mechanisms, Gotts (2003) showed that it was possible to simultaneously address short-lag repetition suppression and priming effects through enhanced synchronization.

span.label: contradicts → the Facilitation model (Henson, 2003; James & Gauthier, 2006; James et al., 2000)
span.quote: Having reviewed four basic proposals as to how repetition suppression might afford repetition priming, the only view that we consider definitively ruled out by current data is the facilitation model, at least in its existing form.

span.label: contradicts → Friston's Bayesian 'explaining away' / predictive coding account (Friston, 2005)
span.quote: Nevertheless, we do not believe that it is self-evident that the brain behaves in its details as a Bayesian neural network model, at least one that relies on anti-symmetrical coupling in the feed-forward versus feedback directions.

span.label: replicates → Gilbert et al. (2010)
span.quote: We found that stimulus repetition led to repetition priming in both patients and increases in low-frequency evoked power (1–15 Hz) for virtually all task-engaged electrodes (i.e., those that exhibited significant evoked responses), replicating the basic pattern of Gilbert et al. (2010).

span.label: neural synchronization —causes→ efficiency
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.9 — **THE ACCOUNT'S LOAD-BEARING STEP, AND `efficiency` IS A BRIDGE TERM RATHER THAN A MEASUREMENT.** `firing MORE SYNCHRONOUSLY with one another, LEADING TO more efficient neural processing` - the verb is explicit and both endpoints are named. Weight 0.9 because the span opens `A very different PROPOSAL that MAY help to resolve this puzzle`: the hedge is the authors' and it is inside the quote. **The edge is real and the thing it connects to behaviour is a word, not a number** - nothing in this paper measures efficiency directly, and the same sentence is where the account stops being physiological and starts being functional.
